## Introduction

`spacy_parse()` returns what spaCy knows about each token: its lemma, its part of speech, its place in the dependency parse. Many questions about a text are about combinations of tokens: a passive verb, an adjective before a noun, a verb with its subject and object. spaCy answers these with *rule-based matching*, which finds the tokens that fit a pattern. In **spacyr**, `spacy_match()` does this, for two kinds of pattern:

- a *token pattern* finds a *sequence of adjacent tokens*, using spaCy's `Matcher`. Words and phrases are matched as sequences too, and are given as in **quanteda**: as a character vector, a `phrase()` object or a dictionary, with wildcards. If words or phrases are what you want to find, go straight to [Words, phrases and dictionaries](#words-phrases-and-dictionaries).
- a *dependency pattern* finds *tokens connected in the dependency parse*, wherever they are in the sentence, using spaCy's `DependencyMatcher`.

Token and dependency patterns are written as R lists, in the structure that spaCy documents in its guide to [rule-based matching](https://spacy.io/usage/rule-based-matching). Whatever the pattern, the result is a data.frame with the same columns. Matching does not change the pipeline or the entities of a document: to turn matches into named entities, see the article on [rule-based named entities](entity_rules.html).


``` r
library("spacyr")
spacy_initialize()
## successfully initialized (spaCy Version: 3.8.18, language model: en_core_web_sm)
```

## Token patterns

A token pattern is a list with one element for each token, and each element is a named list of the attributes that the token must have. This pattern matches the two tokens "new" and "york", in any case:


``` r
txt <- c(d1 = "New York is larger than York. I prefer new York.",
         d2 = "The New York Times is printed in New York.")
spacy_match(txt, list(NY = list(list(LOWER = "new"), list(LOWER = "york"))))
##   doc_id match_id label node sentence_id token_id     text start_id length
## 1     d1        1    NY <NA>           1        1 New York        1      2
## 2     d1        2    NY <NA>           2        3 new York       10      2
## 3     d2        1    NY <NA>           1        2 New York        2      2
## 4     d2        2    NY <NA>           1        8 New York        8      2
```

The name of the pattern, `NY`, is its label. For each match, the result has:

- the document, and `match_id`, the number of the match within the document;
- the label, and `node`, which is `NA` for a sequence and is used by [dependency patterns](#dependency-patterns);
- the sentence and token of the first token of the match, numbered as in `spacy_parse()`;
- the matched text;
- `start_id`, the position of the first token in the document, and `length`, the number of tokens.

Attributes can be any that spaCy sets on a token, including those that the language model assigns: `LEMMA`, `POS` and `TAG` for the part of speech, `DEP` for the dependency relation, and `ENT_TYPE` for the entity type. A token can also have an operator, `OP`, that says how often it may occur: `"?"` for optional, `"+"` for one or more, `"*"` for none or more. This pattern finds nouns with the adjectives before them:


``` r
ball <- "A big red shiny ball and a small blue box."
adj_noun <- list(ADJ_NOUN = list(list(POS = "ADJ", OP = "+"), list(POS = "NOUN")))
spacy_match(ball, adj_noun)
##   doc_id match_id    label node sentence_id token_id               text start_id length
## 1  text1        1 ADJ_NOUN <NA>           1        2 big red shiny ball        2      4
## 2  text1        2 ADJ_NOUN <NA>           1        8     small blue box        8      3
```

### Overlapping matches

More sequences fit that pattern than the two returned: "shiny ball" does, and so do "red shiny ball" and "big red shiny ball". spaCy finds every one of them, and `overlap` says which to keep where the matches of a label overlap. The default, `overlap = "longest"`, keeps the longest; `"first"` keeps the one that starts first; and `"all"` returns every match:


``` r
spacy_match(ball, adj_noun, overlap = "all")
##   doc_id match_id    label node sentence_id token_id               text start_id length
## 1  text1        1 ADJ_NOUN <NA>           1        2 big red shiny ball        2      4
## 2  text1        2 ADJ_NOUN <NA>           1        3     red shiny ball        3      3
## 3  text1        3 ADJ_NOUN <NA>           1        4         shiny ball        4      2
## 4  text1        4 ADJ_NOUN <NA>           1        8     small blue box        8      3
## 5  text1        5 ADJ_NOUN <NA>           1        9           blue box        9      2
```

`overlap` applies to the matches of one label. Matches of different labels can overlap whatever its value.

### Several patterns

A list can hold several patterns, each with its own label. A label can also have alternative patterns, given as a list of token patterns:


``` r
pats <- list(
  ADJ_NOUN = list(list(POS = "ADJ", OP = "+"), list(POS = "NOUN")),
  COLOUR = list(list(list(LOWER = "red")),
                list(list(LOWER = "blue")))
)
spacy_match(ball, pats)
##   doc_id match_id    label node sentence_id token_id               text start_id length
## 1  text1        1 ADJ_NOUN <NA>           1        2 big red shiny ball        2      4
## 2  text1        2   COLOUR <NA>           1        3                red        3      1
## 3  text1        3 ADJ_NOUN <NA>           1        8     small blue box        8      3
## 4  text1        4   COLOUR <NA>           1        9               blue        9      1
```

The values that an attribute may take can be listed with `IN`, so the two colours could also be one pattern, `list(list(LOWER = list(IN = c("red", "blue"))))`. Rows are in the order of the documents and, within a document, of the matches' positions, and `match_id` numbers them in that order.

## Example: passive verbs

Patterns can use the dependency relations that the parser assigns, which makes them a way to find grammatical constructions. The labels of these relations differ between language models, so the first step is to look at how the model in use parses an example. This is `en_core_web_sm`:


``` r
passive_txt <- c(p1 = "The book was written by Jane. Jane wrote the book.",
                 p2 = "Mistakes were made, and the report has not been finished.")
parsed <- spacy_parse(passive_txt, tag = TRUE, dependency = TRUE,
                      lemma = FALSE, entity = FALSE)
parsed[parsed$doc_id == "p1" & parsed$sentence_id == 1, ]
##   doc_id sentence_id token_id   token   pos tag head_token_id   dep_rel
## 1     p1           1        1     The   DET  DT             2       det
## 2     p1           1        2    book  NOUN  NN             4 nsubjpass
## 3     p1           1        3     was   AUX VBD             4   auxpass
## 4     p1           1        4 written  VERB VBN             4      ROOT
## 5     p1           1        5      by   ADP  IN             4     agent
## 6     p1           1        6    Jane PROPN NNP             5      pobj
## 7     p1           1        7       . PUNCT   .             4     punct
```

The English models label the auxiliary of a passive `auxpass`, and tag the past participle `VBN`. A pattern for a passive verb is then a passive auxiliary, any adverbs or negations in between, and a past participle:


``` r
passive <- list(
  PASSIVE = list(list(DEP = "auxpass"),
                 list(DEP = list(IN = c("advmod", "neg")), OP = "*"),
                 list(TAG = "VBN"))
)
spacy_match(passive_txt, passive)
##   doc_id match_id   label node sentence_id token_id          text start_id length
## 1     p1        1 PASSIVE <NA>           1        3   was written        3      2
## 2     p2        1 PASSIVE <NA>           1        2     were made        2      2
## 3     p2        2 PASSIVE <NA>           1       10 been finished       10      2
```

It finds the three passives, and not "Jane wrote the book". Because `sentence_id` and `token_id` are numbered as in `spacy_parse()`, matches can be joined to the parsed tokens on those two columns and `doc_id`:


``` r
matches <- spacy_match(passive_txt, passive)
joined <- merge(matches[, c("doc_id", "sentence_id", "token_id", "text")],
                parsed[, c("doc_id", "sentence_id", "token_id", "token", "dep_rel",
                           "head_token_id")])
joined[order(joined$doc_id, joined$sentence_id, joined$token_id), ]
##   doc_id sentence_id token_id          text token dep_rel head_token_id
## 1     p1           1        3   was written   was auxpass             4
## 3     p2           1        2     were made  were auxpass             3
## 2     p2           1       10 been finished  been auxpass            11
```

The position of a match is that of its first token, which here is the auxiliary, not the verb. The `head_token_id` of the auxiliary is the `token_id` of the verb it belongs to: token 4 of the first sentence of `p1` is "written".

The same columns count the sentences that have a passive in each document. `p2` has two passive matches, but both are in its one sentence, so it counts once:


``` r
table(matches$doc_id)
## 
## p1 p2 
##  1  2
table(unique(matches[, c("doc_id", "sentence_id")])$doc_id)
## 
## p1 p2 
##  1  1
```

## Words, phrases and dictionaries

Words and phrases need no token pattern. They are *lexical patterns*, which describe tokens by their text, and `spacy_match()` takes them as **quanteda**'s functions do, with the same arguments: `valuetype`, which is `"glob"` by default, for wildcards, and `case_insensitive`, which is `TRUE` by default.

### Words

Each element of a character vector describes one token. With the default `valuetype`, `*` stands for any number of characters and `?` for one:


``` r
spacy_match(txt, c("york*", "print*"))
##   doc_id match_id  label node sentence_id token_id    text start_id length
## 1     d1        1  york* <NA>           1        2    York        2      1
## 2     d1        2  york* <NA>           1        6    York        6      1
## 3     d1        3  york* <NA>           2        4    York       11      1
## 4     d2        1  york* <NA>           1        3    York        3      1
## 5     d2        2 print* <NA>           1        6 printed        6      1
## 6     d2        3  york* <NA>           1        9    York        9      1
```

The label of a match is the pattern's text, or its name when it has one; elements with the same name are alternatives for one label:


``` r
spacy_match(txt, c(PLACE = "york", SIZE = "larg*", SIZE = "small*"))
##   doc_id match_id label node sentence_id token_id   text start_id length
## 1     d1        1 PLACE <NA>           1        2   York        2      1
## 2     d1        2  SIZE <NA>           1        4 larger        4      1
## 3     d1        3 PLACE <NA>           1        6   York        6      1
## 4     d1        4 PLACE <NA>           2        4   York       11      1
## 5     d2        1 PLACE <NA>           1        3   York        3      1
## 6     d2        2 PLACE <NA>           1        9   York        9      1
```

`valuetype = "regex"` reads the patterns as regular expressions, and `"fixed"` takes them as they are. `case_insensitive = FALSE` matches case:


``` r
spacy_match(txt, "^(new|york)$", valuetype = "regex", case_insensitive = FALSE)
##   doc_id match_id        label node sentence_id token_id text start_id length
## 1     d1        1 ^(new|york)$ <NA>           2        3  new       10      1
```

Regular expressions are those of Python's `re` module, since spaCy applies them, and not those of R or **quanteda**: `"^\\p{L}+$"` works in **quanteda** and is an error here. A regular expression can match any part of a token, while a glob or a fixed pattern must match all of it.

### Phrases

As in **quanteda**, an element of a character vector is one token even when it contains a space, so `"new york"` finds nothing. A sequence of tokens is given with `quanteda::phrase()`, which splits its argument at the spaces, or as a list of character vectors with one string for each token:


``` r
nrow(spacy_match(txt, "new york"))
## [1] 0
spacy_match(txt, quanteda::phrase("new york*"))
##   doc_id match_id     label node sentence_id token_id     text start_id length
## 1     d1        1 new york* <NA>           1        1 New York        1      2
## 2     d1        2 new york* <NA>           2        3 new York       10      2
## 3     d2        1 new york* <NA>           1        2 New York        2      2
## 4     d2        2 new york* <NA>           1        8 New York        8      2
spacy_match(c(txt, d3 = "Two New Yorkers."), list(NY = c("new", "york*")))
##   doc_id match_id label node sentence_id token_id        text start_id length
## 1     d1        1    NY <NA>           1        1    New York        1      2
## 2     d1        2    NY <NA>           2        3    new York       10      2
## 3     d2        1    NY <NA>           1        2    New York        2      2
## 4     d2        2    NY <NA>           1        8    New York        8      2
## 5     d3        1    NY <NA>           1        2 New Yorkers        2      2
```

These are the matches that **quanteda** finds for the same pattern in spaCy's tokens, which `quanteda::as.tokens()` takes from the output of `spacy_parse()`:


``` r
quanteda::index(quanteda::as.tokens(spacy_parse(txt)), quanteda::phrase("new york*"))
##   docname from to   pattern
## 1      d1    1  2 new york*
## 2      d1   10 11 new york*
## 3      d2    2  3 new york*
## 4      d2    8  9 new york*
```

The strings of a phrase are the tokens: spaCy does not tokenize them again. So they match only where spaCy made the same tokens of the text, and spaCy's tokens are not always those that the spaces suggest. `spacy_tokenize()` shows them:


``` r
acme <- "She joined Acme, Inc. last year."
spacy_tokenize(acme)[[1]]
## [1] "She"    "joined" "Acme"   ","      "Inc."   "last"   "year"   "."
nrow(spacy_match(acme, quanteda::phrase("Acme, Inc.")))
## [1] 0
spacy_match(acme, quanteda::phrase("Acme , Inc."))[, c("label", "text", "start_id", "length")]
##         label       text start_id length
## 1 Acme , Inc. Acme, Inc.        3      3
```

The collocations that `quanteda.textstats::textstat_collocations()` finds can be given as they are. Each is the sequence of its words, which are matched as they are, as **quanteda** matches collocations: only `case_insensitive` applies to them.

`valuetype` and `case_insensitive` apply to lexical patterns only. Token patterns and dependency patterns say how they match through their attributes, and the phrases of an `as_entity_patterns()` object each have their own setting, so giving either argument with only such patterns is an error, rather than being ignored.

### Phrases that spaCy tokenizes

To have spaCy split a phrase into tokens, as it splits the text, give the phrase as an `as_entity_patterns()` object, which records the label of each phrase and whether it matches exactly or in any case. Unlike the patterns above, these match exactly by default:


``` r
spacy_match(txt, as_entity_patterns(c(PLACE = "New York")))
##   doc_id match_id label node sentence_id token_id     text start_id length
## 1     d1        1 PLACE <NA>           1        1 New York        1      2
## 2     d2        1 PLACE <NA>           1        2 New York        2      2
## 3     d2        2 PLACE <NA>           1        8 New York        8      2
spacy_match(acme, as_entity_patterns(c(ORG = "Acme, Inc.")))[, c("label", "text", "start_id", "length")]
##   label       text start_id length
## 1   ORG Acme, Inc.        3      3
```

### Dictionaries

A **quanteda** dictionary can be given directly. Its top-level keys become the labels, so the values under nested keys take the label of the top-level key above them. Its values match in any case, with wildcards as in **quanteda**, unless `valuetype` or `case_insensitive` say otherwise:


``` r
dict <- quanteda::dictionary(list(place = c("new york", "york"),
                                  size = c("larg*", "small*", "big*")))
spacy_match(txt, dict)
##   doc_id match_id label node sentence_id token_id     text start_id length
## 1     d1        1 place <NA>           1        1 New York        1      2
## 2     d1        2  size <NA>           1        4   larger        4      1
## 3     d1        3 place <NA>           1        6     York        6      1
## 4     d1        4 place <NA>           2        3 new York       10      2
## 5     d2        1 place <NA>           1        2 New York        2      2
## 6     d2        2 place <NA>           1        8 New York        8      2
```

Since "york" is itself a value, it also matches inside each "New York". With the default, `overlap = "longest"`, such a nested match of the same key is dropped, which is what `quanteda::tokens_lookup()` does with its own default, `nested_scope = "key"`. For this dictionary and these texts, the number of matches of each label is then the count that `tokens_lookup()` gives for that key, when it is applied to spaCy's tokens, which `quanteda::as.tokens()` takes from the output of `spacy_parse()`. Each match of a dictionary value is one row, so `table()` counts matches. With `overlap = "all"`, the nested matches are counted too:


``` r
table(spacy_match(txt, dict)$label)
## 
## place  size 
##     5     1
spacy_tokens <- quanteda::as.tokens(spacy_parse(txt))
quanteda::featfreq(quanteda::dfm(quanteda::tokens_lookup(spacy_tokens, dict)))
## place  size 
##     5     1
table(spacy_match(txt, dict, overlap = "all")$label)
## 
## place  size 
##     9     1
```

The two agree whenever they start from the same candidate matches under the same keys, since they then choose among overlapping matches by the same rule. Using spaCy's tokens for both does not guarantee that:

- A value without a wildcard is a phrase, which spaCy's tokenizer splits into tokens, while **quanteda** splits every value at its spaces. The value `"Acme, Inc."` is the three tokens `Acme`, `,` and `Inc.` for `spacy_match()`, which finds it; `tokens_lookup()` looks for a token `Acme,` and finds nothing:


``` r
acme_dict <- quanteda::dictionary(list(ORG = "Acme, Inc."), tolower = FALSE)
spacy_match(acme, acme_dict)[, c("label", "text", "start_id", "length")]
##   label       text start_id length
## 1   ORG Acme, Inc.        3      3
quanteda::tokens_lookup(quanteda::as.tokens(spacy_parse(acme)), acme_dict)
## tokens of 1 document (0 tokens, 1 type).
## text1 :
## character(0)
```

- For a dictionary with nested keys, the labels here are the top-level keys, which corresponds to `tokens_lookup(levels = 1)`. Its default, `levels = 1:5`, counts nested keys such as `place.us` separately.

The counts can also differ from a lookup on `quanteda::tokens(txt)`, because the tokens are then **quanteda**'s and not spaCy's. What `spacy_match()` adds to a lookup is where each match is, in a form that joins to the output of `spacy_parse()`. A dictionary's phrases and wildcard values can be combined with token patterns by converting it with `as_entity_patterns()` and joining the two with `c()`. To have the values of a dictionary split at their spaces, as **quanteda** does, give them with `phrase()`.

`quanteda::kwic()` follows another rule than `tokens_lookup()`, which no value of `overlap` gives: it drops a match only when all of its tokens are in another match, of any pattern. It would drop a "New York" that lies inside another label's "New York Times", which `overlap = "longest"` keeps, since labels are separate; and it would keep both of two matches of one label that partly overlap, where `overlap = "longest"` keeps one.

The phrases of an `as_entity_patterns()` object, and dictionary values without a wildcard, are split into tokens by spaCy's tokenizer, and match the same sequence of tokens in a text. spaCy sometimes splits a word differently in another case: it keeps `"Inc."` as one token, but splits `"inc."` into two. So a phrase written as `"acme widgets, inc."` does not match the text `"Acme Widgets, Inc."` even when it matches in any case, while the phrase `"Acme Widgets, Inc."` does:


``` r
inc <- "We wrote to Acme Widgets, Inc. yesterday."
nrow(spacy_match(inc, as_entity_patterns(c(ORG = "acme widgets, inc."),
                                         case_insensitive = TRUE)))
## [1] 0
spacy_match(inc, as_entity_patterns(c(ORG = "Acme Widgets, Inc."),
                                    case_insensitive = TRUE))
##   doc_id match_id label node sentence_id token_id               text start_id length
## 1  text1        1   ORG <NA>           1        4 Acme Widgets, Inc.        4      4
```

## Dependency patterns

A token pattern finds tokens that are next to each other. The parts of a grammatical construction often are not: the subject of a passive verb can be many words before it. A *dependency pattern* describes tokens by their relations in the parse instead. It is a list of nodes, and each node is a named list with:

- `RIGHT_ID`, a name for the node;
- `RIGHT_ATTRS`, the attributes of the token, as in a token pattern;
- for every node but the first, `LEFT_ID`, the name of an earlier node, and `REL_OP`, the relation between that node and this one. `">"` means that this node is a direct dependent of the earlier one.

A dependency pattern goes in the same named list as a token pattern, and `spacy_match()` tells the two apart by these keys. This pattern is a past participle, with a passive subject and a passive auxiliary as its dependents:


``` r
passive_dep <- list(
  list(RIGHT_ID = "verb", RIGHT_ATTRS = list(TAG = "VBN")),
  list(LEFT_ID = "verb", REL_OP = ">", RIGHT_ID = "subject",
       RIGHT_ATTRS = list(DEP = "nsubjpass")),
  list(LEFT_ID = "verb", REL_OP = ">", RIGHT_ID = "aux",
       RIGHT_ATTRS = list(DEP = "auxpass"))
)
m <- spacy_match(passive_txt, list(PASSIVE = passive_dep))
m
##   doc_id match_id   label    node sentence_id token_id     text start_id length
## 1     p1        1 PASSIVE    verb           1        4  written        4      1
## 2     p1        1 PASSIVE subject           1        2     book        2      1
## 3     p1        1 PASSIVE     aux           1        3      was        3      1
## 4     p2        1 PASSIVE    verb           1        3     made        3      1
## 5     p2        1 PASSIVE subject           1        1 Mistakes        1      1
## 6     p2        1 PASSIVE     aux           1        2     were        2      1
## 7     p2        2 PASSIVE    verb           1       11 finished       11      1
## 8     p2        2 PASSIVE subject           1        7   report        7      1
## 9     p2        2 PASSIVE     aux           1       10     been       10      1
```

The columns are the same as for a sequence, but a match now has one row for each node of the pattern, each for a single token. `node` says which part of the pattern the token matched, and the rows of a match share its `match_id`, so that `doc_id` and `match_id` together identify a match. Unlike the token pattern, this one also returns the subject of each passive, and finds the subject "report" although three words separate it from its verb.

To get one row for each match, with a column for each node, reshape the result:


``` r
wide <- reshape(m[, c("doc_id", "match_id", "node", "text")],
                idvar = c("doc_id", "match_id"), timevar = "node",
                direction = "wide")
names(wide) <- sub("^text\\.", "", names(wide))
wide
##   doc_id match_id     verb  subject  aux
## 1     p1        1  written     book  was
## 4     p2        1     made Mistakes were
## 7     p2        2 finished   report been
```

A pattern can follow the parse further. Adding the agent, "by" and its object, finds who did what to what, for the passives that say so:


``` r
agent <- c(passive_dep, list(
  list(LEFT_ID = "verb", REL_OP = ">", RIGHT_ID = "by",
       RIGHT_ATTRS = list(DEP = "agent")),
  list(LEFT_ID = "by", REL_OP = ">", RIGHT_ID = "agent",
       RIGHT_ATTRS = list(DEP = "pobj"))
))
m <- spacy_match(passive_txt, list(PASSIVE_AGENT = agent))
m[m$node %in% c("subject", "verb", "agent"), c("doc_id", "node", "text")]
##   doc_id    node    text
## 1     p1    verb written
## 2     p1 subject    book
## 5     p1   agent    Jane
```

Each label has one dependency pattern, so alternatives, such as passives with and without an agent, get labels of their own. The other relations that `REL_OP` can take, such as `">>"` for a dependent at any depth and `"."` for the next token, are listed in spaCy's [documentation](https://spacy.io/usage/rule-based-matching#dependencymatcher). `overlap` does not apply to dependency patterns: every match is returned, whatever its value.

### Both kinds of pattern together

A list can hold token patterns and dependency patterns, each under its own label. They are matched in one pass over the texts, and the matches come back in one table:


``` r
both <- spacy_match(passive_txt["p1"], c(passive, list(CLAUSE = passive_dep)))
both
##   doc_id match_id   label    node sentence_id token_id        text start_id length
## 1     p1        1 PASSIVE    <NA>           1        3 was written        3      2
## 2     p1        2  CLAUSE    verb           1        4     written        4      1
## 3     p1        2  CLAUSE subject           1        2        book        2      1
## 4     p1        2  CLAUSE     aux           1        3         was        3      1
```

Within a document, matches are in the order of the position of their first row, which for a dependency pattern is the token of its first node, and `match_id` numbers the two kinds together. A match is a distinct pair of `doc_id` and `match_id`, not a row: `both` has two matches in four rows. `overlap` applies to the token patterns of such a list. Every row is a span of tokens with a `start_id` and a `length`, so the rows of both kinds can be handled alike: here, to look up each in the output of `spacy_parse()`.


``` r
parsed_p1 <- parsed[parsed$doc_id == "p1", ]
cbind(both[, c("match_id", "label", "node", "text")],
      first_token = parsed_p1$token[both$start_id])
##   match_id   label    node        text first_token
## 1        1 PASSIVE    <NA> was written         was
## 2        2  CLAUSE    verb     written     written
## 3        2  CLAUSE subject        book        book
## 4        2  CLAUSE     aux         was         was
```

## Matches in context

`quanteda::kwic()` shows each occurrence of a pattern with the tokens around it. It can do the same for positions found elsewhere, given as an *index*, and `as_index()` makes one from the output of `spacy_match()`. The positions in a table of matches count spaCy's tokens, with its tokens of whitespace, so the tokens to give `kwic()` are those of `spacy_parse()` for the same texts, and not those of `quanteda::tokens()`:


``` r
spacy_tokens <- quanteda::as.tokens(spacy_parse(txt))
m <- spacy_match(txt, dict)
quanteda::kwic(spacy_tokens, index = as_index(m), window = 3)
## Keyword-in-context with 6 matches.
##                                                          
##    [d1, 1:2]                | New York | is larger than  
##    [d1, 4:4]    New York is |  larger  | than York.      
##    [d1, 6:6] is larger than |   York   | . I prefer      
##  [d1, 10:11]     . I prefer | new York | .               
##    [d2, 2:3]            The | New York | Times is printed
##    [d2, 8:9]  is printed in | New York | .
```

The index has one row for each row of the matches, in the same order, so the other columns of the matches can be put beside the concordance. For a dependency pattern, that says which node each line is:


``` r
dep <- spacy_match(passive_txt, list(CLAUSE = passive_dep))
kw <- quanteda::kwic(quanteda::as.tokens(parsed), index = as_index(dep), window = 2)
cbind(dep[, c("match_id", "node")], as.data.frame(kw)[, c("docname", "pre", "keyword", "post")])
##   match_id    node docname           pre  keyword        post
## 1        1    verb      p1      book was  written     by Jane
## 2        1 subject      p1           The     book was written
## 3        1     aux      p1      The book      was  written by
## 4        1    verb      p2 Mistakes were     made       , and
## 5        1 subject      p2               Mistakes   were made
## 6        1     aux      p2      Mistakes     were      made ,
## 7        2    verb      p2      not been finished           .
## 8        2 subject      p2       and the   report     has not
## 9        2     aux      p2       has not     been  finished .
```

A concordance made this way shows the matches that `spacy_match()` returned, chosen by `overlap` where they overlap. That is not always what `kwic()` finds when it searches for the same patterns itself, since its rule is another, as described [above](#dictionaries): here it leaves out the "York" inside each "New York", which belongs to another pattern, where `overlap = "all"` keeps them.


``` r
all_matches <- spacy_match(txt, quanteda::phrase(c("new york", "york")), overlap = "all")
nrow(quanteda::kwic(spacy_tokens, index = as_index(all_matches)))
## [1] 9
nrow(quanteda::kwic(spacy_tokens, quanteda::phrase(c("new york", "york"))))
## [1] 5
```

`as_index()` also takes the output of `spacy_extract_entity()` and of `spacy_extract_nounphrases()`, whose positions are counted in the same way:


``` r
quanteda::kwic(spacy_tokens, index = as_index(spacy_extract_entity(txt)), window = 3)
## Keyword-in-context with 4 matches.
##                                                                 
##    [d1, 1:2]               |      New York      | is larger than
##  [d1, 10:11]    . I prefer |      new York      | .             
##    [d2, 1:4]               | The New York Times | is printed in 
##    [d2, 8:9] is printed in |      New York      | .
```

## Counting matches

`quanteda::tokens_lookup()` replaces the tokens of each document by the keys of the dictionary values found in it, and a document-feature matrix of the result counts each key in each document. The matches of `spacy_match()` give the same kind of object in two steps. The first keeps one row for each match, which is a distinct pair of `doc_id` and `match_id`. The second splits the labels by document, and makes tokens of them:


``` r
m <- spacy_match(txt, dict)
m1 <- m[!duplicated(m[c("doc_id", "match_id")]), ]
labels <- quanteda::as.tokens(split(m1$label, factor(m1$doc_id, levels = names(txt))))
labels
## tokens of 2 documents (6 tokens, 2 types).
## d1 :
## [1] "place" "size"  "place" "place"
## 
## d2 :
## [1] "place" "place"
quanteda::dfm(labels, tolower = FALSE)
## dfm of 2 documents x 2 features (6 occurrences, 25.00% sparsity).
##     features
## docs place size
##   d1     3    1
##   d2     2    0
```

Three details matter:

- The levels of the factor are the names of all the documents, so a document without a match stays in the result, with no tokens. Without them, `split()` would leave it out. For a corpus, the names are `quanteda::docnames(x)`.
- `tolower = FALSE` keeps the labels as they are: `dfm()` would otherwise put a label such as `PASSIVE` in lower case.
- The matrix has a column for each label that was found. `tokens_lookup()` gives one for every key, also for a key that matched nothing; `quanteda::dfm_match(x, names(dict))` adds those, in the order of the dictionary.

For this dictionary and these texts, the result is the matrix that `tokens_lookup()` gives on spaCy's tokens, since the two find the same candidate matches under the same keys, as described [above](#dictionaries):


``` r
quanteda::dfm(quanteda::tokens_lookup(spacy_tokens, dict))
## dfm of 2 documents x 2 features (6 occurrences, 25.00% sparsity).
##     features
## docs place size
##   d1     3    1
##   d2     2    0
```

The first step matters for dependency patterns, whose matches have one row for each node. Counting rows would count each passive clause here three times:


``` r
dep <- spacy_match(passive_txt, list(CLAUSE = passive_dep))
table(dep$doc_id, dep$label)
##     
##      CLAUSE
##   p1      3
##   p2      6
dep1 <- dep[!duplicated(dep[c("doc_id", "match_id")]), ]
quanteda::dfm(quanteda::as.tokens(split(dep1$label, factor(dep1$doc_id, levels = names(passive_txt)))),
              tolower = FALSE)
## dfm of 2 documents x 1 feature (3 occurrences, 0.00% sparsity).
##     features
## docs CLAUSE
##   p1      1
##   p2      2
```

## What to keep in mind

**Labels belong to the model.** The tags and dependency labels above are those of spaCy's English models. Other languages' models use other labels, and some do not mark the passive at all. Look at the output of `spacy_parse(x, tag = TRUE, dependency = TRUE)` for the model you use before writing a pattern.

**A match is only as good as the parse.** The model tags and parses by prediction, and makes mistakes. It also makes choices that a pattern has to follow. Here the second verb of a coordination, "edited", is attached to the first as `conj` and has no subject or auxiliary of its own, so neither passive pattern above finds it:


``` r
coord <- "The book was written and edited by Jane."
spacy_match(coord, c(passive, list(CLAUSE = passive_dep)))[, c("label", "node", "text")]
##     label    node        text
## 1 PASSIVE    <NA> was written
## 2  CLAUSE    verb     written
## 3  CLAUSE subject        book
## 4  CLAUSE     aux         was
```

A further pattern, for a participle coordinated with a passive verb, finds it:


``` r
conj <- list(
  list(RIGHT_ID = "first", RIGHT_ATTRS = list(TAG = "VBN")),
  list(LEFT_ID = "first", REL_OP = ">", RIGHT_ID = "aux",
       RIGHT_ATTRS = list(DEP = "auxpass")),
  list(LEFT_ID = "first", REL_OP = ">", RIGHT_ID = "verb",
       RIGHT_ATTRS = list(TAG = "VBN", DEP = "conj"))
)
spacy_match(coord, list(PASSIVE_CONJ = conj))[, c("node", "text")]
##    node    text
## 1 first written
## 2   aux     was
## 3  verb  edited
```

Testing patterns on examples of the constructions you want, and of those you do not, is the way to find such cases.

**The pipeline has to set what a pattern asks for.** A pattern on `DEP` needs the parser, and a dependency pattern needs a dependency parse; both give an error without one, which stops the call, whatever other patterns were given with them. A pattern on `ENT_TYPE` gives a warning when no component sets entities, as after `spacy_initialize(entity = FALSE)`, since it would match nothing.

## Speed

Matching adds little to the time that spaCy takes to parse the texts. On a test with 5,000 sentences, a dictionary of 10,000 phrases and several hundred wildcard values took no longer than a single token pattern. Token patterns are slower in large numbers, since spaCy checks each one against the text: give phrases as lexical patterns or as phrases, not as token patterns, when there are thousands of them. Lexical patterns without a wildcard or a regular expression are matched as phrases are, by spaCy's `PhraseMatcher`; those with one become token patterns, of which the single words are combined into one pattern for each label.

Patterns that do not use entities are faster after `spacy_initialize(entity = FALSE)`, which leaves out the named entity recognizer. `spacy_initialize()` does nothing while spaCy is running, as it has been since the start of this article, so call `spacy_finalize()` first:


``` r
spacy_finalize()
spacy_initialize(entity = FALSE)
## successfully initialized (spaCy Version: 3.8.18, language model: en_core_web_sm)
spacy_match(passive_txt, passive)
##   doc_id match_id   label node sentence_id token_id          text start_id length
## 1     p1        1 PASSIVE <NA>           1        3   was written        3      2
## 2     p2        1 PASSIVE <NA>           1        2     were made        2      2
## 3     p2        2 PASSIVE <NA>           1       10 been finished       10      2
spacy_finalize()
```

See the article on [improving performance](performance.html) for more on this, and for `n_process` and `batch_size`, which `spacy_match()` also takes.
